115066.e: For animals, the genus name and species name may be the same, as with the red fox Vulpes vulpes. For plants this is not allowed.
115066.m: For animals, the genus and species name may be the same.

115067.q: In which language are scientific names such as Picea abies for the spruce mostly formed?
115067.e: Scientific names are formed from Latin or Greek. Picea abies is the spruce, the most common tree in Swiss forests.
115067.m: Scientific species names are mostly Latin.

115068.q: What do you do in a vegetation survey?
a: Note down all the plant species in an area
Dig up a tree and weigh it
115068.e: In a vegetation survey you choose a marked-out area and note down all the plant species in it. For each species you estimate how much of the area it covers.
115068.m: In a vegetation survey you note down all the plant species in an area.

115069.q: Which aid do you need in a vegetation survey to name unknown plants?
115069.e: With an identification book or an identification app, you can find out what a plant is called from its flowers and leaves. Only then can you note it down.
115069.m: Unknown plants are identified with an identification book.

115070.q: What do you estimate for each plant species in a vegetation survey?
115070.e: The cover shows what proportion of the area the plants of a species cover when seen from above. This shows which species are dominant.
115070.m: In a vegetation survey you estimate the cover of each species.

115071.q: A plant species covers 3 of the 4 square metres of a survey area. What is its cover?
115071.e: 3 out of 4 is three quarters. Three quarters is 75 per cent of the area.
115071.m: The cover shows what proportion of the area a species covers.

115072.q: What does it mean if a plant species has a very low cover?
a: It covers only a tiny part of the area
It covers almost the whole area
115072.e: The cover shows how much of the area a species covers when seen from above. A very low value means that only a few small plants of this species are present.
115072.m: A low cover shows a species that is rare in the area.

115073.q: Which layer is the lowest in a forest vegetation survey?
115073.e: In a forest, from top to bottom, you distinguish the tree, shrub, herb and moss layers. The cover is estimated separately for each layer.
115073.m: The moss layer is the lowest layer in the forest.

115074.q: Why must the area of a vegetation survey not be too small?
a: Otherwise many typical species are missing
Otherwise the plants do not grow
Otherwise it cannot rain on it
Otherwise the area is too hard to find
115074.e: On an area that is too small you only record some of the species. Only from a certain size are almost all the typical species present.
115074.m: A survey area must be big enough for all the typical species to be in it.

115075.q: Why do you mark out the area of a vegetation survey precisely, for example with string and pegs?
a: So that you only count species inside it
So that animals do not walk into it
So that the plants grow faster
So that the soil does not dry out
115075.e: Surveys can only be compared if there is a clear boundary. Species outside the area are not noted down.
115075.m: A marked-out area makes vegetation surveys comparable.

115076.q: Why are plant indicator values useful for experts?
a: You can judge the soil without measuring equipment
You can tell the time with them
You can tell the age of the plants
You can use them to sell plants
115076.e: If you know which plants grow where, you can work out from the plants present how moist, acidic or nutrient-rich the soil is.
115076.m: Indicator values help to judge the soil from the plants.

115077.q: What does a plant's indicator value show?
a: The conditions it usually grows in
How much it costs in a shop
115077.e: Indicator values show where a species is usually found, for example damp or dry, acidic or rich in lime. So you can work out what a site is like from its plants.
115077.m: An indicator value tells you the conditions a plant grows in.

115078.q: What does the moisture value (F) describe among the ecological indicator values?
115078.e: The moisture value shows how dry or wet the soil is where the plant typically grows. A low value means dry, a high value wet.
115078.m: The moisture value shows how damp the soil is.

115079.q: What does the reaction value (R) describe among the indicator values?
a: How acidic or rich in lime the soil is
115079.e: The reaction value describes the acidity of the soil. Low values show acidic soils, high values alkaline soils, often rich in lime.
115079.m: The reaction value shows how acidic the soil is.

115081.q: Four species grow in an area with moisture values of 2, 3, 4 and 3. What is the average moisture value?
115081.e: You add the values and divide by the number of species: (2 + 3 + 4 + 3) ÷ 4 = 12 ÷ 4 = 3. The average describes the area as moderately damp.
115081.m: The average indicator value is the mean of the values of all the species.

115082.q: What does the light value (L) describe among the indicator values?
115082.e: The light value shows whether a species tends to grow in the shade or in bright, open places. A low value means shady, a high value very bright.
115082.m: The light value shows how much light a plant needs.

115083.q: A plant has the highest moisture value. Where is it most likely to grow?
a: In a swamp or on a shore
115083.e: A high moisture value means that the plant needs wet soil. Such species grow in swamps, bogs and on shores.
115083.m: A high moisture value means a wet site.

a: Only professors are allowed to do research
Research only takes place in the laboratory
115084.e: In citizen science, interested people without specialist training collect data for research. Experts then analyse the data.
115084.m: In citizen science, non-experts help with research.

115085.q: What is the national data and information centre for the flora of Switzerland, to which you can report plant finds, called?
115085.e: Info Flora collects reports of finds from experts and non-experts. The data help to show how widespread and how endangered plants in Switzerland are.
115085.m: Plant finds in Switzerland are reported to Info Flora.

a: A short event where you find as many species as possible
A thunderstorm over a nature reserve
A quick method of drying plants
A race along a nature trail
115086.e: In a BioBlitz, experts and non-experts search an area together for a short time, often 24 hours, looking for as many animal and plant species as possible. This gives a snapshot of biodiversity.
115086.m: In a BioBlitz you look for as many species as possible in a short time.

115087.q: Which details make a plant record especially valuable for research?
a: Name and address of your parents
115087.e: With the place and date, a record can be put on a map and into a time series. A photo allows experts to check the identification.
115087.m: A good record includes the place, date and a photo.

115088.q: Why do experts check records from citizen science projects?
a: To punish the people who sent them
To count plants that do not exist
115088.e: Non-experts sometimes mix up similar species. Checking keeps the data reliable enough for research.
115088.m: Experts check citizen science data so that it stays reliable.

115089.q: In phenology, where non-experts can also help with research, what do you observe?
a: When plants come into leaf and flower
115089.e: Phenology records when in the year, for example, the hazel flowers or the beech gets its leaves. Records over many years show the effects of the climate.
115089.m: Phenology records when plants flower and come into leaf.

115090.q: Which photo is best if you want an identification app to recognise a plant?
a: Sharp close-ups of the flower and leaf
A blurred picture from far away
A photo of the whole meadow against the light
115090.e: Apps compare features such as flower shape and leaf edge with many reference pictures. The sharper and closer these features can be seen, the more reliable the result.
115090.m: Identification apps need sharp close-ups of the flower and leaf.

115091.q: What is the biggest advantage when many volunteers collect data for a research project?
a: You get data from a large area
The data are always free of mistakes
115091.e: Researchers on their own could never observe in so many places at the same time. Many volunteers provide data over large areas and many years.
115091.m: Thanks to many volunteers, research gets data from large areas.

115092.q: Which institution does the Botanical Garden in Bern belong to?
115092.e: The Botanical Garden of Bern is part of the University of Bern. It is used for teaching, research and by the public.
115092.m: The Botanical Garden of Bern belongs to the University of Bern.

115093.q: Which river is the Botanical Garden of Bern on?
115093.e: The garden lies on a sunny slope above the Aare in the Altenberg district. From there you look down on the river.
115093.m: The Botanical Garden of Bern lies on the slope above the Aare.

115095.q: Roughly how many plant species does the Botanical Garden of Bern show?
115095.e: According to the garden, around 5,500 different plant species from all over the world grow there. They include native species as well as tropical plants.
115095.m: Around 5,500 plant species grow in the Botanical Garden of Bern.

115096.q: How much does it cost to visit the Botanical Garden of Bern?
115096.e: The garden and the glasshouses can be visited free of charge. This makes it a popular place to relax in the middle of the city.
115096.m: The Botanical Garden of Bern can be visited for free.

115097.q: What does the Botanical Garden of Bern show in its alpine garden?
115097.e: An alpine garden is a rock garden with plants from the Alps and other mountains. This lets you see mountain plants without climbing a mountain.
115097.m: Plants from the mountains grow in the alpine garden.

115098.q: Which glasshouse is there in the Botanical Garden of Bern?
115098.e: Palms, ferns and succulents, among others, grow in the glasshouses. It is warm there even in winter.
115098.m: You can visit a palm house in the Botanical Garden of Bern.

115099.q: Apart from showing plants, what job does a university garden such as the Botanical Garden of Bern have?
115099.e: Botanical gardens collect plants for teaching and research. They also help to preserve rare and endangered species.
115099.m: Botanical gardens are used for research and for preserving rare plants.

115100.q: Roughly how old is the botanical garden in Geneva?
115100.e: The botanical garden in Geneva was founded in 1817. In 2017 it celebrated its 200th anniversary.
115100.m: The botanical garden in Geneva is over 200 years old.

115101.q: Which language is mainly spoken in Geneva, where the Jardin botanique is?
115101.e: Geneva lies in western Switzerland, where French is spoken. That is why the garden is called “Jardin botanique”.
115101.m: Geneva is in the French-speaking part of Switzerland.

115102.q: Which lake is the botanical garden in Geneva on?
115102.e: The garden lies on the right bank of Lake Geneva, not far from the Palais des Nations.
115102.m: The botanical garden in Geneva is on Lake Geneva.

115103.q: What is a herbarium, like the one the botanical garden in Geneva has?
a: A collection of pressed, dried plants
115103.e: In a herbarium, plants are pressed, dried, labelled and stored. The Geneva herbarium, with over six million specimens, is one of the largest in the world.
115103.m: A herbarium is a collection of dried plants.

115104.q: Roughly how big is the botanical garden in Geneva?
115104.e: The garden covers around 28 hectares. That is about the size of 40 football pitches.
115104.m: The botanical garden in Geneva covers around 28 hectares.

115105.q: Why did the botanical garden in Geneva move from the old town to the lake in 1904?
a: The plants wanted a lake view
The old garden became a railway station
115105.e: At first the garden was in the old town in the Parc des Bastions. In 1904 it moved to its present, much larger site on Lake Geneva.
115105.m: The botanical garden in Geneva moved to the lake because it needed more space.

115106.q: Who owns the Conservatoire et Jardin botaniques de Genève?
115106.e: The full name is “Conservatoire et Jardin botaniques de la Ville de Genève”. So it is an institution of the City of Geneva.
115106.m: The botanical garden in Geneva is an institution of the City of Geneva.

115107.q: What does “Conservatoire” mean in the name of the Geneva institution?
a: The part with the herbarium and research
115107.e: In the Conservatoire, plants are preserved and studied, mainly in the herbarium and the library. The Jardin is the public garden.
115107.m: In the Geneva Conservatoire, plant collections are preserved and studied.

115108.q: What is a field notebook in nature research?
115108.e: In a field notebook you record observations directly out in the field. That way no information is lost before you get home.
115108.m: In a field notebook you note down observations right there outdoors.

115109.q: What is the best thing to write with in a field notebook so that nothing smudges when it rains?
115109.e: Pencil does not run when it gets wet and stays readable for a long time. Ink can smudge in the rain.
115109.m: In a field notebook you write in pencil, because it does not run in the rain.

115110.q: What do you note down first for each observation in a field notebook?
115110.e: Without the date and place, you cannot make sense of an observation later. Then come details such as species, number and habitat.
115110.m: Every field observation needs a date and place.

115111.q: How can you give a place of finding especially precisely in a field notebook?
a: With the name of the weather
With the colour of the sky
115111.e: Coordinates, for example from a mobile phone or a national map, describe a place very precisely. This means you can find the spot again later.
115111.m: Coordinates let you give a place of finding precisely.

115112.q: Why do people often draw small sketches in a field notebook?
a: Drawing is compulsory in the forest
115112.e: When you draw, you look more closely and record the shapes of leaves or flowers. A sketch can also show what remains unclear in a photo.
115112.m: Sketches in a field notebook help to record features precisely.

115113.q: When should you write observations in your field notebook?
a: At the end of the holidays
115113.e: Memories quickly become inaccurate. If you write things down straight away, you reliably record details such as number, time or location.
115113.m: You write observations in the field notebook straight away, on the spot.

115114.q: What is a collection number in a field notebook for, when you also collect plants for a herbarium?
a: It links the note and the specimen
It shows the price of the plant
It counts the steps you have walked
It gives the number of flowers
115114.e: Each plant collected gets a number that is also written in the field notebook. This way you know later which notes belong to which specimen.
115114.m: A collection number links the herbarium specimen with the notes in the field notebook.

115115.q: On which ship did Charles Darwin keep many field notebooks on his voyage around the world?
115115.e: Darwin sailed around the world on HMS Beagle from 1831 to 1836. His notebooks later formed the basis for many discoveries.
115115.m: Charles Darwin filled many field notebooks on the Beagle.

115116.q: Why do you see a three-dimensional image through a stereo microscope?
a: Each eye has its own light path
It always magnifies a thousand times
115116.e: A stereo microscope has a separate light path for each eye with a slightly different angle of view. The brain puts the two images together into a three-dimensional impression.
115116.m: Thanks to two light paths, the stereo microscope shows a three-dimensional image.

115117.q: Which lighting do you usually use with a stereo microscope to look at a whole flower?
115117.e: Objects that light cannot pass through, such as flowers, seeds or insects, are lit from above. The light is reflected from the surface.
115117.m: With a stereo microscope, objects are usually lit from above.

115118.q: What do you usually not need with a stereo microscope, unlike an ordinary light microscope?
115118.e: With a stereo microscope you look at whole objects. With a microscope where light shines through, on the other hand, specimens must be thin enough for light to pass through.
115118.m: With a stereo microscope you can look at whole objects without thin slices.

115119.q: What else is a stereo microscope often called in Swiss schools?
115119.e: Because you look into it with both eyes at the same time, it is often called a binocular. “Bini” is Latin and means two at a time.
115119.m: A stereo microscope is often called a binocular, because you look with both eyes.

115120.q: How strongly does a stereo microscope magnify compared with a light microscope for cells?
115120.e: A stereo microscope usually only magnifies up to about a hundred times, often much less. To see single cells you need a light microscope with stronger magnification.
115120.m: A stereo microscope magnifies less than a light microscope for cells.

115121.q: Why is it easy to work with tweezers and a needle under a stereo microscope?
a: It has a large working distance
115121.e: There is plenty of space between the lens and the object. That is why you can, for example, take a flower apart under the microscope.
115121.m: The large working distance allows dissecting under the stereo microscope.

115122.q: How does the image in a stereo microscope appear compared with the object?
a: Upright and the right way round
115122.e: Prisms in the stereo microscope turn the image so that it appears upright and the right way round. If you move the object to the left, it also moves to the left in the image.
115122.m: In a stereo microscope the image is upright and the right way round.

115123.q: Which of these objects is best examined with a stereo microscope?
115123.e: Whole small objects such as flowers, seeds or tiny moss plants are ideal. Bacteria, viruses and atoms are far too small for it.
115123.m: With a stereo microscope you examine whole small objects.

115221.q: What is the smallest unit that shows all the features of life?
115221.e: A cell can feed, grow, react to stimuli and reproduce. Atoms and molecules are not alive, and organs are made of many cells.
115221.m: The cell is the smallest living unit.

115222.q: With which instrument were the first cells discovered?
115222.e: Cells are far too small for the naked eye. Only with the microscope did people see small chambers in the 17th century, for example in cork.
115222.m: Cells were discovered with the microscope.

115223.q: Which green cell organelle carries out photosynthesis in plant cells?
115223.e: Chloroplasts contain the green pigment chlorophyll. With it the plant turns light energy into sugar.
115223.m: Chloroplasts make plant cells green and carry out photosynthesis.

115224.q: What is the liquid called that fills the inside of the cell?
115224.e: Cytoplasm is a jelly-like liquid. The cell organelles are found in it.
115224.m: The cell organelles float in the cytoplasm.

115225.q: Roughly how many cells make up the body of an adult human?
115225.e: Estimates are around 30 to 40 trillion cells. Most of them are red blood cells.
115225.m: A human is made of trillions of cells.

115226.q: Which living things consist of just one single cell?
115226.e: Bacteria are single-celled organisms. Earthworms, ferns and jellyfish are multicellular.

115227.q: Roughly how big is a typical human body cell?
a: About a hundredth of a millimetre
About a millionth of a millimetre
115227.e: Most body cells measure about 10 to 30 micrometres. That is about one to three hundredths of a millimetre, which is why you need a microscope.
115227.m: Most cells cannot be seen with the naked eye.

115228.q: What does a bacterial cell lack compared with a human cell?
115228.e: In bacteria, the genetic information lies freely in the cytoplasm. Humans, animals, plants and fungi, on the other hand, have cells with a nucleus.

115229.q: Which germs are not made of cells?
115229.e: Viruses have no metabolism of their own and can only multiply in other cells. That is why they are usually not counted as living things.

115230.q: What is the main job of the cell nucleus?
a: It controls the cell and contains the genetic information
It protects the cell from the outside
115230.e: The genetic information is in the nucleus. From there, the processes in the cell are controlled.
115230.m: The nucleus is the control centre of the cell.

115231.q: In what form is the genetic information stored in the nucleus?
115231.e: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a long molecule. Its building blocks form the blueprint for the cell's proteins.
115231.m: Genetic information is stored in DNA.

115232.q: Why are cells often stained with dye before looking at them under the microscope?
a: So the nucleus and cell parts are easier to see
So the cells do not dry out
So the microscope does not break
115232.e: Many parts of the cell are almost transparent. Dyes collect especially in the nucleus and make it easy to see.
115232.m: With dye, the nucleus is easier to see.

115233.q: Which human blood cells have no nucleus when mature?
115233.e: Red blood cells lose their nucleus as they mature. This gives them more room for the red blood pigment that carries oxygen.
115233.m: Mature red blood cells have no nucleus.

115234.q: What does the nucleus usually look like under the microscope?
a: Like a round body inside the cell
Like a thread outside the cell
Not at all, it is invisible
115234.e: The nucleus is usually the largest part inside the cell. It appears as a round or oval body.
115234.m: The nucleus is a round body inside the cell.

115235.q: Which thread-like structures become visible in the nucleus when the cell prepares to divide?
115235.e: Before division, the DNA is tightly wound up and packed. Then you can see it under the microscope as chromosomes.
115235.m: Chromosomes are packed threads of DNA.

115236.q: What job does the cell membrane have?
a: It separates the cell and controls the exchange of substances
115236.e: The cell membrane surrounds every cell. It decides which substances get in and out.
115236.m: The cell membrane is the boundary of the cell.

115237.q: What do we call the property of the cell membrane of letting only certain substances through?
115237.e: Experts also say selectively permeable. Small particles like water get through, many other substances only by special routes.

115238.q: What is the movement of particles from a place of high to a place of low concentration called?
115238.e: Particles are constantly moving randomly. As a result they spread out evenly over time, for example a drop of ink in water.
115238.m: In diffusion, particles spread out evenly by themselves.

115239.q: Which particles pass especially easily straight through the fatty layer of the cell membrane?
115239.e: Very small, fat-soluble particles such as oxygen and carbon dioxide simply slip through the membrane. Large or charged particles need special routes.
115239.m: Small gas particles pass through the membrane easily.

115240.q: What happens to a red blood cell in pure water?
a: It takes in water, swells and can burst
It gives off water and shrinks
It becomes as hard as glass
115240.e: There are more dissolved particles in the cell than in pure water. So water flows in until the cell bursts.
115240.m: Cells in pure water take in water.

115241.q: Which building blocks in the cell membrane act like gates for certain substances?
115241.e: The membrane contains proteins that form channels or pumps. Through them, for example, sugar and salts get into the cell.
115241.m: Membrane proteins are the gates of the cell.

115242.q: What is transport through the membrane called that uses energy and pumps substances against the concentration gradient?
115242.e: In active transport, protein pumps in the membrane do the work. The cell needs energy for this, for example in the sodium-potassium pump.
115242.m: Active transport costs the cell energy.

115243.q: Which cell organelle is often called the “powerhouse of the cell”?
115243.e: In this organelle, energy for the cell is obtained from nutrients. Hence the comparison with a power station.
115243.m: Mitochondria are the powerhouses of the cell.

115244.q: Which process takes place in the mitochondria?
115244.e: In cellular respiration, sugar is broken down step by step. This releases energy that the cell can use.
115244.m: Cellular respiration takes place in the mitochondria.

115245.q: Which gas do the mitochondria need for cellular respiration?
115245.e: We breathe in oxygen with our lungs, and the blood carries it to every cell. Without it, mitochondria cannot break down sugar completely.

115246.q: Which molecule do mitochondria make as an energy carrier for the cell?
115246.e: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the energy currency of the cell. Muscles need it, for example, to contract.
115246.m: ATP is the energy currency of the cell.

115247.e: Mature red blood cells have neither a nucleus nor mitochondria. This leaves lots of room for the red blood pigment that carries oxygen.
115247.m: Red blood cells have no mitochondria.

115248.q: In which cells do you find especially many mitochondria?
115248.e: The heart muscle works non-stop and needs a great deal of energy. A large part of its cell volume consists of mitochondria.
115248.m: Cells with high energy needs have many mitochondria.

a: It has two membranes, the inner one heavily folded
It has only one smooth membrane
It has no membrane at all
It has a cell wall made of cellulose
115249.e: The inner membrane forms many folds. This creates a large surface for the processes that produce energy.
115249.m: Mitochondria have a folded inner membrane.

115250.q: Which theory says that mitochondria were once independent bacteria?
115250.e: According to this theory, bacteria were taken in by larger cells a very long time ago. They lived on inside them and became organelles.

115251.q: What is nuclear division in normal body cells called?
115251.e: In mitosis, the nucleus of a body cell divides. Then the cytoplasm divides too.
115251.m: Body cells divide their nucleus by mitosis.

115252.q: How many daughter cells are formed in mitosis followed by cell division?
115252.e: One parent cell becomes two daughter cells. These can later grow and divide again themselves.
115252.m: In mitosis, one cell becomes two.

115253.q: How does the genetic information of the daughter cells after mitosis compare with that of the parent cell?
115253.e: Each daughter cell receives a complete copy of all the chromosomes. So the daughter cells are genetically identical.
115253.m: After mitosis, both cells have the same genetic information.

115254.q: What must happen to the DNA before cell division?
115254.e: The DNA is copied before division. This copying process is called replication.
115254.m: Before every division, the DNA is copied.

115255.q: A bacterial cell divides every 20 minutes. How many cells have come from one cell after 2 hours?
115255.e: 2 hours are 120 minutes, which gives 120 ÷ 20 = 6 divisions. The number doubles each time: 2 to the power of 6 is 64.
115255.m: With every division, the number of bacteria doubles.

115256.q: What is a disease called in which cells divide uncontrollably and can form tumours?
115256.e: Normally, cell division is strictly controlled. If this control fails, malignant tumours can develop.

115257.q: What does the body need cell division for?
a: For growth and replacing old cells
For gas exchange in the lungs
115257.e: Through cell division, children grow and wounds heal. In addition, dead cells, for example in the skin, are constantly replaced.
115257.m: Cell division makes growth and healing possible.

115258.q: What does a cell do most of the time between two divisions?
a: It grows and does its jobs
It travels through the whole body
115258.e: The division itself only takes a short time. For most of the time the cell grows, works and copies its DNA for the next division.
115258.m: Between divisions, the cell grows and works.

115259.q: What does biology mean by a tissue?
a: A group of similar cells with the same job
115259.e: Many similar cells work together and form a tissue. Several tissues together make up an organ.
115259.m: A tissue is made of many similar cells.

115260.q: Which tissue covers the surface of the body and lines cavities?
115260.e: Epithelial tissue forms, for example, the top layer of skin and the lining of the gut. It protects and can take in or release substances.

115261.q: Which group of tissues do bone and cartilage belong to?
115261.e: Bone and cartilage give the body support and shape. That is why they count as connective and supporting tissue.
115261.m: Bone and cartilage are supporting tissues.

115262.q: Which muscle tissue works involuntarily and without a break for a whole lifetime?
115262.e: Heart muscle tissue contracts rhythmically without us controlling it. Skeletal muscles, on the other hand, we move on purpose.
115262.m: Heart muscle tissue works without a break.

115263.q: Which tissue carries electrical signals through the body?
115263.e: Nervous tissue consists of nerve cells and supporting cells. It passes on information at lightning speed.

115264.q: With which instrument can you make the cells of a tissue visible?
115264.e: Cells are so small that you cannot see them with the naked eye. Under the microscope you can see how the cells in a tissue are arranged.
115264.m: Tissue is examined with the microscope.

115265.q: Which tissue shapes the outer ear and covers the surfaces of joints?
115265.e: Cartilage is firm but flexible and smooth. That is why you can bend your outer ear, and joints glide well.
115265.m: Cartilage is firm and flexible at the same time.

a: A body part made of different tissues with a particular job
A single cell with a nucleus
115267.e: An organ such as the heart is made of muscle, connective, nervous and epithelial tissue. Together they carry out a job.
115267.m: An organ is made of several types of tissue.

115268.q: Which organ in the upper left abdomen breaks down old red blood cells?
115268.e: The spleen filters the blood and sorts out old red blood cells. It also helps with the body's defences.
115268.m: The spleen breaks down old red blood cells.

115269.q: Which organ is the largest gland in the human body?
115269.e: In adults the liver weighs about 1.5 kilograms. It makes bile, breaks down toxins and stores nutrients.
115269.m: The liver is the largest gland.

115270.q: Which organ has three lobes on the right and two on the left?
115270.e: The right lung has three lobes, the left one only two. That is because the heart needs room on the left.
115270.m: The left lung is smaller because of the heart.

115271.q: Which organ in the neck makes hormones that control metabolism?
115271.e: The thyroid gland is at the front of the neck below the larynx. It needs iodine for its hormones, which is why table salt in Switzerland is iodised.
115271.m: The thyroid gland controls metabolism with hormones.

115272.q: In which organ are most nutrients absorbed into the blood?
115272.e: The wall of the small intestine has countless villi and therefore a huge surface. There the digested nutrients pass into the blood.
115272.m: Nutrients pass into the blood in the small intestine.

115273.e: In the retina of the eye there are sensory cells for light and colours. They turn light into nerve signals.
115273.m: The eye is the sense organ for light.

115274.q: What is the transfer of an organ from one person to another called?
115274.e: In a transplant, for example, a kidney is donated. In Switzerland the Swisstransplant foundation coordinates organ donation.
115274.m: Transferring an organ is called a transplant.

a: Several organs that carry out a job together
115275.e: An organ system links different organs into a team. All the organ systems together form the organism.
115275.m: Several organs together form an organ system.

115276.q: Which organ system do the mouth, stomach and intestines belong to?
115276.e: In the digestive system, food is broken up and split into nutrients. These then pass into the blood.
115276.m: Mouth, stomach and intestines belong to the digestive system.

115277.q: Which organ system do the heart and blood vessels belong to?
115277.e: The heart pumps blood through arteries, capillaries and veins. In this way oxygen and nutrients reach every cell.
115277.m: The heart and blood vessels form the cardiovascular system.

115278.q: What does the musculoskeletal system consist of?
115278.e: Bones give support, muscles pull on them through tendons, and ligaments hold the joints together. Together they make movement possible.
115278.m: Bones and muscles together form the musculoskeletal system.

115279.q: Which two organ systems work together so that oxygen reaches the muscles?
115279.e: The lungs take in oxygen from the air. The blood then carries it to the muscles with the help of the heart.
115279.m: Breathing and circulation together supply the cells with oxygen.

115280.q: Which organ system controls the body with messenger substances in the blood?
115280.e: Glands such as the pituitary gland or the adrenal glands release hormones into the blood. These messengers act on places far away in the body.
115280.m: The hormone system works with messenger substances.

115281.q: Which organ system do the kidneys and bladder belong to?
115281.e: The kidneys make urine, which flows through the ureters into the bladder. In this way waste substances are removed.
115281.m: The kidneys and bladder belong to the urinary system.

115282.q: What is the science of the structure of the body and its organs called?
115282.e: Anatomy describes where organs are and how they are built. Physiology, on the other hand, studies how they work.
115282.m: Anatomy studies the structure of the body.

115283.q: Which organ system do the windpipe, bronchi and lungs belong to?
115283.e: Through these organs, air reaches the tiny air sacs in the lungs. There oxygen passes into the blood.
115283.m: The windpipe and lungs belong to the respiratory system.

115284.q: A microscope has a 10x eyepiece and a 40x objective. What is the total magnification?
115284.e: The total magnification is the product of the two magnifications. 10 times 40 is 400.
115284.m: You multiply the magnifications of the eyepiece and the objective.

115285.q: What is the lens of the microscope called that you look into with your eye?
115285.e: It is also called the ocular, from the Latin “oculus” for eye. It magnifies the image once more.
115285.m: The eyepiece is next to the eye.

115286.q: What is the lens of the microscope called that sits directly above the specimen?
115286.e: The objective faces the object. Often several objectives sit on a rotating nosepiece.
115286.m: The objective is next to the specimen.

115287.q: Up to roughly what magnification is a light microscope usefully usable?
115287.e: Because of the wavelength of light, finer details can no longer be told apart. More than about 1000x to 1500x does not show any extra detail.
115287.m: A light microscope usefully magnifies up to about 1000x.

115288.q: Which Dutchman discovered tiny living things in the 17th century using microscopes he built himself?
115288.e: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground very good lenses. He was one of the first to observe single-celled organisms and bacteria.
115288.m: Van Leeuwenhoek was one of the first to observe bacteria.

115289.q: Which part of the microscope focuses the light onto the specimen?
115289.e: The condenser sits under the stage. It collects the light from the lamp and directs it through the specimen.

115290.q: What is the thin glass plate called on which you place a specimen?
115290.e: The specimen is placed on the slide and usually covered with a cover slip. Then it goes on the stage.
115290.m: Specimens are placed on a slide.

115291.q: Which parts of a cell can you see well with a school light microscope?
115291.e: The nucleus and cell wall are big enough for the light microscope. For tiny structures such as ribosomes you need an electron microscope.
115291.m: You can already see the nucleus with a light microscope.

115292.q: Which knob do you use first to bring the image roughly into focus on a microscope?
115292.e: With the coarse focus knob you move the stage or tube in big steps. Then you focus precisely with the fine focus knob.

115293.q: What does a growth chart for children show?
a: Height or weight depending on age
The number of cells in the blood
How long you sleep each night
115293.e: At each check-up, a measurement is marked on the chart. In this way you can see how a child develops over the years.
115293.m: A growth chart shows development over age.

115294.q: What has the biggest influence on a child's eventual adult height?
115294.e: Height is to a large extent inherited. So from the parents' height you can estimate a rough target height.
115294.m: Adult height depends strongly on the parents.

115295.q: Roughly how much does a baby grow in its first year of life?
115295.e: In the first year of life you grow faster than in any later year. Even the growth spurt in the teenage years is much slower.
115295.m: In its first year a baby grows about 25 centimetres.

115296.q: Roughly how does a baby's weight change in its first year of life?
115296.e: A baby gains a lot of weight in its first year. On its first birthday it usually weighs about three times as much as at birth.
115296.m: By the first birthday, weight roughly triples.

115297.q: On average, how much does a child grow per year at primary school age?
115297.e: Between early childhood and puberty, growth is quite even. Each year usually adds about 5 to 6 centimetres.
115297.m: Schoolchildren grow about 5 to 6 centimetres a year.

115300.q: How much does a newborn baby in Switzerland weigh on average?
115300.e: Most babies weigh between 2.5 and 4.5 kilograms at birth. The average is about 3.3 kilograms.
115300.m: A newborn weighs about 3.3 kilograms on average.

115301.q: A child's height is on the 75th percentile. What does that mean?
a: 75 out of 100 children of the same age are the same height or shorter
75 out of 100 children of the same age are taller
The child has reached 75 per cent of its adult height
115301.e: Percentiles compare a child with many children of the same age. On the 75th percentile, about three quarters are the same height or shorter.
115301.m: Percentiles compare a child with others of the same age.

115302.q: Which percentile is exactly the median, in other words the middle?
115302.e: At the median, half the values are below and the other half above. That is the 50th percentile.

115303.q: A child is on the 97th percentile. About how many out of 100 children of the same age are taller?
115303.e: 97 out of 100 are the same height or shorter. So 100 minus 97 leaves 3 children who are taller.
115303.m: On the 97th percentile, only a few are taller.

115304.q: During a growth check, what can be a sign that further tests are needed?
a: The child moves clearly away from their percentile curve
The child always stays on the same percentile
The child is on the 50th percentile
The child grows the same way as their brothers and sisters
115304.e: What matters is that a child roughly follows their own curve. A clear change up or down is looked at by a doctor.
115304.m: A child should roughly follow their own percentile curve.

115305.q: Why are there separate percentile charts for girls and boys?
a: Because they grow at different speeds and to different heights
115305.e: On average, girls and boys have different growth patterns and adult heights. That is why they are compared using their own charts.
115305.m: Girls and boys have their own growth charts.

115306.q: What percentage of children are between the 3rd and the 97th percentile?
115306.e: 3 per cent are below the 3rd percentile, and 3 per cent are above the 97th. That leaves 100 minus 3 minus 3, which is 94 per cent.
115306.m: The vast majority of children are between the 3rd and 97th percentile.

115307.q: What is a percentile in general?
a: A value that divides ordered data into a hundred equal parts
115307.e: The word comes from “per centum”, meaning “out of a hundred”. Percentiles divide a series of data sorted by size into 100 sections.
115307.m: Percentiles divide data into a hundred parts.

115308.q: In a group of 20 children, the heights are distributed exactly as in the population. How many children are below the 25th percentile?
115308.e: 25 per cent of 20 children is 20 times 0.25. That makes 5 children.
115308.m: A quarter of the group is below the 25th percentile.

115309.q: At what stage of life do young people have a clear growth spurt?
115309.e: After childhood, you suddenly grow faster again at this stage of life. After that, growth slows down quickly.
115309.m: There is a growth spurt during puberty.

115310.q: On average, who reaches the big teenage growth spurt earlier?
a: Both at exactly the same time
115310.e: On average, girls reach their growth spurt about two years earlier than boys. That is why girls are often taller at 11 or 12.
115310.m: Girls usually have their growth spurt earlier than boys.

115311.q: How much can a teenager grow per year at the peak of the growth spurt?
115311.e: At the peak, many teenagers grow almost twice as fast as in their primary school years. Boys usually grow a bit more than girls.
115311.m: During the growth spurt you grow up to about 10 centimetres a year.

115313.q: Why are teenagers often especially hungry during a growth spurt?
a: Because the body needs lots of energy and building materials for growth
115313.e: New bones, muscles and organs have to be built. For this the body needs more energy and nutrients than usual.

115314.q: Why do teenagers sometimes seem a bit clumsy during a growth spurt?
a: Because their sense of their body first has to get used to the new lengths
115314.e: Arms and legs get longer in a short time. The brain needs some time to adjust movements to them.
115314.m: After a growth spurt, your sense of your body has to adjust.

115315.q: Which parts of the body usually grow first in the teenage growth spurt?
115315.e: Growth usually starts with the hands and feet. Then come the arms and legs, and finally the torso.
115315.m: Hands and feet often grow first in the spurt.

115316.q: Which mineral is especially important for building bones during the growth spurt?
115316.e: Calcium is a main building block of bones. It is found, for example, in dairy products, mineral water and green vegetables.

121627.q: Which native bird is a well-known brood parasite?
121627.e: The female cuckoo lays her eggs in other birds' nests. The host birds raise the cuckoo chick, often at the expense of their own young.
121627.m: The cuckoo has its young raised by other birds.

123401.q: Which plants are typical of the Arctic tundra?
123401.e: Only low plants that can cope with cold and a short growing season grow in the tundra. Dwarf willows and dwarf birches hardly reach knee height.
123401.m: The tundra is dominated by mosses, lichens and dwarf shrubs.

124408.q: What colour is grade A on the Nutri-Score?
124408.e: A is dark green and stands for the best nutritional composition. E is red.
124408.m: A dark green A is the best Nutri-Score grade.

125400.q: Where does the energy stored in biomass originally come from?
a: From geothermal heat deep inside the Earth
From nuclear fission in the ground
125400.e: Plants convert sunlight into chemical energy and store it in sugar, starch and cellulose. This energy is released again when it is burnt.

126114.q: The fruits of which plant served as George de Mestral's model?
126114.e: Burdock fruits have lots of tiny hooks and get caught in fur and clothes. This is how animals spread their seeds.
126114.m: Burdock was the model for Velcro.

126120.q: Which two parts does a Velcro fastener consist of?
126120.e: One strip has tiny hooks, the other soft loops. When pressed together they hook into each other; when pulled apart they come undone again.
126120.m: A Velcro fastener consists of hooks and loops.

126163.e: Urban gardening means growing vegetables, herbs and flowers in cities. It is often done together with others on waste ground, roofs or in backyards.
126163.m: Urban gardening is gardening in the city.

126179.q: Which winter road treatment is especially harmful to city trees along roads?
126179.e: Road salt gets into the soil with meltwater and damages roots and leaves. The trees then take up water and nutrients less well.
126179.m: Road salt harms the roots of city trees.

126393.q: Which number do you dial in Switzerland for the ambulance emergency line when an ambulance needs to go to hospital?
126393.e: 144 is the number for the ambulance emergency line. 117 is the police, 118 the fire brigade and 143 the helpline Dargebotene Hand.
126393.m: In Switzerland you dial 144 for an ambulance.

127766.q: What does the abbreviation HTML stand for?
127766.e: Written out, HTML means Hypertext Markup Language. With HTML you describe how web pages are built up.
127766.m: HTML is the basis from which web pages are built.

127767.q: What kind of language is HTML?
127767.e: With HTML you mark up content, for example: this is a heading, this is a paragraph. There are no loops or calculations in HTML as there are in a programming language.
127767.m: HTML describes the structure of a page, but it does not calculate anything.

127768.e: The British physicist Tim Berners-Lee developed HTML together with the World Wide Web. At the time he was working at the CERN research centre.
127768.m: Tim Berners-Lee is considered the inventor of HTML and the World Wide Web.

127769.q: What goes between <body> and </body> in an HTML document?
a: The visible content of the page
127769.e: Everything in the body element is shown by the browser in the window. This includes texts, pictures, links and forms.
127769.m: What is in the body is what you see on the web page.

127770.q: Which file extension does a typical HTML file have?
127770.e: HTML files usually end in .html, sometimes also .htm. The home page of a website is often called index.html.
127770.m: You can recognise an HTML file by the extension .html.

127771.q: Which line does a modern HTML5 document usually begin with?
127771.e: The line <!DOCTYPE html> tells the browser that it is an HTML5 document. It goes right at the start of the file.
127771.m: An HTML5 document begins with <!DOCTYPE html>.

127772.q: Which program is enough for writing HTML code?
127772.e: HTML is plain text. So you can write it in any simple text editor and save it as an .html file.
127772.m: A simple text editor is enough for HTML.

127773.q: What is the content between <head> and </head> in an HTML document called?
127773.e: The head section contains information about the page, for example the title and the character encoding. This information is usually not shown directly on the page.
127773.m: The head section contains information about the page, not the visible content.

127774.q: What is CSS responsible for on a web page?
127774.e: With CSS you set colours, fonts, spacing and the layout. HTML supplies the structure, CSS the design.
127774.m: CSS decides how a web page looks.

127775.q: What does the abbreviation CSS stand for?
127775.e: CSS means Cascading Style Sheets. Cascading means that several rules work together according to a fixed order of priority.
127775.m: CSS are design rules that work according to an order of priority.

127776.q: Which CSS property changes the text colour?
127776.e: The property color sets the font colour, for example color: red. The other properties control alignment, spacing and borders.
127776.m: In CSS you set the text colour with color.

127777.q: Which CSS property sets the background colour?
127777.e: With background-color you colour the background of an element. There is no property called text-color in CSS.
127777.m: You colour the background with background-color.

127778.q: What do you use a class such as .important for in CSS?
a: To give many elements the same design
To make the page load faster
127778.e: A class selector such as .important targets all elements with class="important". This way you design many elements with a single rule.
127778.m: In CSS you write classes with a full stop in front.

127779.q: How often should an ID such as id="title" appear on a web page?
127779.e: An ID is like a name that belongs to only one element. In CSS you target it with a hash sign, for example #title.
127779.m: In CSS you select an ID with the hash sign.

127780.q: Which CSS property changes the font size?
127780.e: With font-size you set how big a text appears, for example font-size: 20px. The other names are not valid CSS properties.
127780.m: You set the font size with font-size.

127781.q: What is the difference between margin and padding in CSS?
a: margin is the outer spacing, padding the inner spacing
margin is the colour, padding the font
margin is the border, padding the shadow
margin only applies to pictures, padding only to text
127781.e: In the box model, padding lies between the content and the border, margin outside the border. This lets you control spacing exactly.
127781.m: Padding is inside, margin is outside.

127782.q: Where do you usually include an external CSS file in the HTML page?
a: In the head section with the link element
Right at the end in the footer element
127782.e: With <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css"> in the head section a CSS file is loaded. This way the design applies to the whole page.
127782.m: You link a CSS file in the head section with the link element.

127783.q: Which HTML element makes the largest heading?
127783.e: Headings go from <h1> to <h6>, with <h1> being the most important and largest. <h6> is the smallest level.
127783.m: The most important heading on a page goes in h1.

127784.q: Which HTML element stands for a paragraph of text?
127784.e:
The p stands for paragraph. The text goes between

and

.
127784.m: In HTML a paragraph is marked up with p.

127785.q: Which HTML element do you use to include a picture?
127785.e: The element shows a picture; you give the picture file in the src attribute. It needs no closing tag.
127785.m: In HTML you include pictures with img.

127786.q: Which attribute of describes the picture in words for people who cannot see it?
127786.e: The alternative text in the alt attribute is read aloud by screen readers, for example. It also appears if the picture cannot be loaded.
127786.m: Every picture needs a descriptive alt text.

127787.q: Which HTML element creates an unordered list with bullet points?
127787.e: ul stands for unordered list. The individual entries each go in <li> elements.
127787.m: A list with bullet points begins with ul.

127788.q: Which HTML element do you use for a numbered list?
127788.e: ol stands for ordered list. The browser numbers the entries automatically.
127788.m: You write a numbered list with ol.

127789.e: stands for break and starts a new line without starting a new paragraph. It has no closing tag.
127789.m: With br you force a line break.

127790.q:
How do you write the closing tag for

?
127790.e: A closing tag has a slash after the angle bracket. Together with the opening tag it surrounds the content.
127790.m: A closing tag starts with a slash after the bracket.

127791.q: Which HTML element sets the text shown in the browser tab?
127791.e: The <title> element goes in the head section. Its content appears in the tab and also in search engine results.
127791.m: The text in the browser tab comes from the title element.

127792.q: Which HTML element do you use to create a link?
127792.e: The a stands for anchor. The text between and becomes clickable.
127792.m: In HTML you write links with the a element.

127793.q: Which attribute contains the destination of a link?
127793.e: The href attribute contains the address the link leads to. href comes from hypertext reference.
127793.m: The destination of a link goes in the href attribute.

127794.q: What does target="_blank" do on a link?
a: The page opens in a new tab
127794.e: With target="_blank" the browser opens the destination in a new tab or window. The original page stays open.
127794.m: With target="_blank" a link opens a new tab.

a: A link that points from the location of the current page
A link with a complete web address
A link that only works on Sundays
A link to a telephone number
127795.e: A relative link such as pictures/photo.html gives the path starting from the current file. An absolute link contains the complete address with the domain.
127795.m: Relative links describe the path from the current page.

127796.q: What is a link called that no longer works because the destination is missing?
127796.e: A dead link leads nowhere; often the error message 404 then appears. Websites should be checked regularly for dead links.
127796.m: A dead link points to a page that no longer exists.

127797.q: Which link destination makes a click open the email program?
127797.e: A link such as <a href="mailto:info@example.ch"> opens a new email window with the address. This lets people get in touch.
127797.m: A link with mailto opens the email program.

127798.q: How do you link to a particular place with id="contact" on the same page?
127798.e: A hash sign with the ID name jumps to the matching place on the page. This is called a jump link or anchor.
127798.m: With a hash sign a link jumps to a place on the page.

127799.q: What is text called that is connected to other texts by links?
127799.e: Hypertext is text with references to other texts. You jump from one text to the next with a click.
127799.m: Texts connected by links are called hypertext.

127800.q: What is the main job of a web browser?
127800.e: A browser loads HTML, CSS, pictures and scripts from servers and uses them to display the web page. Well-known browsers include Firefox, Chrome and Safari.
127800.m: A web browser fetches web pages and shows them.

127801.q: What does the address bar of a web browser show?
a: The address of the page that is open
127801.e: The address bar shows the URL of the current page, for example https://www.example.ch. You can also type in an address there yourself.
127801.m: The address bar shows the URL of the current page.

127802.q: What is Apple's web browser called?
127802.e: Safari comes pre-installed on iPhones, iPads and Macs. Edge comes from Microsoft and Chrome from Google.
127802.m: Apple's web browser is called Safari.

127803.q: What does a browser do with the HTML code of a web page?
a: It turns it into a visible page
It deletes it without reading it
It sends it to all your contacts
127803.e: The browser reads the code and works out how texts, pictures and buttons should look. Then it shows the finished page.
127803.m: The browser turns code into a visible page.

127804.q: What does a browser store in its cache?
a: Copies of loaded files for faster access
127804.e: The browser keeps pictures, scripts and other files in the cache. If you visit the page again, it does not need to download them again.
127804.m: The cache makes familiar pages load faster.

127805.q: What is a cookie in connection with web browsers?
a: A small file with data from a website
127805.e: Websites use cookies to store small pieces of information in the browser, such as whether you are logged in. Some cookies are also used to track users across several sites.
127805.m: Cookies are small packets of data that websites put in the browser.

127806.q: What are the developer tools in a browser for?
a: To examine the code of a page and find errors
127806.e: With the developer tools you can look at and test a page's HTML, CSS and JavaScript. In many browsers you open them with the F12 key.
127806.m: Developer tools help you examine web pages.

127807.q: What does a browser's private or incognito mode do?
a: History and cookies are deleted after closing
You are completely invisible on the internet
127807.e: In private mode the browser does not keep history and cookies after closing. Websites, your school or your internet provider can still see what you do.
127807.m: Private mode only protects on your own device, not on the whole internet.

127808.q: Which country ending does Switzerland have in internet addresses?
127808.e: .ch comes from Confoederatio Helvetica, the Latin name for Switzerland. .cz is the ending for Czechia.

127809.q: What is the last part of a domain, such as .ch or .com, called?
127809.e: The top-level domain is at the far right of a domain. There are country endings like .ch and general ones like .com or .org.
127809.m: The ending of a domain is called the top-level domain.

127810.q: Which system translates domain names into IP addresses?
127810.e: DNS works like the internet's telephone directory. For a name like example.ch it finds the matching IP address of the server.
127810.m: The DNS is the telephone directory of the internet.

127811.q: Which ending belongs to the Principality of Liechtenstein?
127811.e: .li is the country ending for Liechtenstein. .lt belongs to Lithuania and .lu to Luxembourg.

127812.q: In the address school.example.ch, what is the part “school”?
127812.e: A subdomain goes to the left of the actual domain. It lets you separate areas of a website, such as shop.example.ch.
127812.m: Whatever is to the left of the domain is a subdomain.

127813.q: What do you have to do to get your own domain?
a: Have it registered with a provider
Simply type it into the browser
Apply for it from the Federal Council
Enter it in the telephone directory
127813.e: Domains are registered through registrars and usually paid for every year. In Switzerland a .ch domain usually costs only a few francs a year.
127813.m: You have to register and pay for your own domain.

127814.q: Which ending was originally meant for commercial websites?
127814.e: .com stands for commercial. .edu is used for universities in the USA and .gov for US authorities.

127815.q: What happens if two people want to register the same domain?
a: Only one person can get it
Both get it at the same time
The domain automatically gets a number
127815.e: Every domain is unique worldwide. Usually whoever registers it first gets it.

127816.q: What does a web server do?
a: It delivers web pages to browsers
It shows web pages on the screen
It writes new web pages automatically
127816.e: A web server waits for requests from browsers and sends back the files they want. The browser then shows them.
127816.m: A web server answers requests from browsers.

127817.q: What does the abbreviation HTTP stand for?
127817.e: HTTP is the protocol that browsers and web servers use to exchange data. It sets out what requests and responses look like.
127817.m: HTTP is the language between browser and web server.

127819.q: Which error code shows that a page was not found?
127819.e: The status code 404 means Not Found. The code 500, on the other hand, means an error on the server.
127819.m: The error 404 means the page was not found.

127820.q: Why is a web server usually switched on day and night?
a: So that the website can be reached at any time
So that it does not break
So that it uses less electricity
So that it writes web pages itself
127820.e: Browsers all over the world can request a page at any time of day. If the server is switched off, it cannot answer.
127820.m: A web server runs all the time so that websites can always be reached.

127821.q: What is the principle called in which a browser requests something and a server answers?
127821.e: The browser is the client that requests something. The server provides the data and answers.
127821.m: On the web the client asks and the server answers.

127822.q: Which software is a well-known web server?
127822.e: The Apache HTTP Server is widely used, free web server software. Thunderbird is an email program, Audacity an audio program.
127822.m: Apache is well-known web server software.

127823.q: What does a web hosting provider offer?
a: Storage space and servers for websites
127823.e: A web host provides storage on servers that are permanently connected to the internet. This means you do not have to run your own server.
127823.m: With web hosting you rent space on a server for your website.

a: A website is printed on paper
You share your password with friends
A website only runs on your own phone
127824.e: With shared hosting, many websites are on the same server. This is cheap, but the performance is shared.
127824.m: With shared hosting many websites share one server.

127825.q: What is it called when you rent a whole server just for yourself?
127825.e: A dedicated server is available to only one customer. It offers more performance and control, but costs more.
127825.m: A whole server just for yourself is called a dedicated server.

127826.q: Which protocol is traditionally used to upload files to web space?
127826.e: FTP means File Transfer Protocol and is used to transfer files. Today people often use the encrypted version, SFTP.
127826.m: Files are often uploaded to the server by FTP or SFTP.

127827.q: Where are web hosts' servers usually located?
127827.e: Data centres provide cooling, emergency power and fast internet connections. This keeps the websites reliably reachable.
127827.m: Web servers are usually in well-secured data centres.

127828.q: In web hosting, what does the storage space figure mean?
a: How much data you may store on the server
How many visitors arrive per second
127828.e: Storage space limits how big all the files of the website may be together. Pictures and videos need especially a lot of space.
127828.m: Storage space tells you how much data fits on the web space.

127829.q: Why is the location of the data centre important for some Swiss companies?
a: Because of data protection under Swiss law
Because websites would otherwise be displayed wrongly
Because otherwise the .ch domain is forbidden
Because the colours would otherwise look different
127829.e: If a server is in Switzerland, Swiss law applies to the data. That is why some companies deliberately choose hosting in Switzerland.
127829.m: The server location affects which data protection law applies.

127830.q: What is a backup in web hosting?
a: A safety copy of the website data
127830.e: A backup is a safety copy. If something breaks or gets deleted, you can use it to restore the website.
127830.m: Regular backups protect a website from losing data.

127831.q: What does responsive web design mean?
a: The page adapts to the screen size
The page is only black and white
127831.e: With responsive web design, the content rearranges itself depending on the device. That way a page is easy to read on a phone, tablet and computer.
127831.m: Responsive pages look good on every screen.

127832.q: Which CSS technique do you use to react to different screen widths?
127832.e: With a media query such as @media (max-width: 600px), certain rules only apply on narrow screens. That way you can adapt the layout.
127832.m: Media queries adapt the layout to the screen width.

127833.q: What does the Mobile First approach mean?
a: You design for small screens first
You only test on the computer
127833.e: With Mobile First, you plan the view for smartphones first. Then you extend the layout for bigger screens.
127833.m: Mobile First means starting with the smallest screen.

127834.q: What often happens when a web page is not responsive and you open it on a phone?
a: It becomes tiny or sticks out over the edge
It cannot be opened at all
127834.e: A page built only for big screens does not fit on a narrow phone. You then have to zoom or swipe sideways.
127834.m: Without responsive design, pages are hard to read on phones.

127835.q: Which width setting for a picture adapts to the width of the screen?
a: Half the width of the window
127835.e: A setting relative to the window width grows and shrinks with the screen. Fixed sizes such as 800 pixels are often too wide on a phone.
127835.m: Relative widths adapt to the screen.

127836.q: Why are widths in responsive layouts often given in per cent?
a: So that elements adapt to the available width
So that the page loads faster
So that the colours become stronger
So that the text becomes bold
127836.e: A width of 50% is always half as wide as the surrounding element. Fixed pixel widths, on the other hand, often do not fit on small screens.

127837.q: Which CSS layout system arranges elements in rows and columns like a grid?
127837.e: With display: grid you create a grid of rows and columns. It is well suited to responsive layouts.
127837.m: CSS Grid arranges content in a grid.

127838.q: Which CSS layout model arranges elements flexibly in a row or column?
127838.e: With display: flex you spread elements out in a row or column. With flex-wrap they can move to the next line when there is little space.
127838.m: Flexbox arranges elements flexibly in one direction.

127839.q: What do you call the screen width at which a responsive layout changes?
127839.e: At a breakpoint, for example at 768 pixels, the layout switches, say, from one column to two columns. The page then looks different on a phone than on a computer.
127839.m: At a breakpoint the layout changes.

127840.q: What is the aim of an accessible internet?
a: Everyone should be able to use websites
127840.e: Accessible websites can also be used by people with visual, hearing or other impairments. Often everyone else benefits too.

a: A program that reads out what is on the screen
127841.e: Blind and visually impaired people have content read out by a screen reader or shown on a Braille display. For this, the page needs a clean structure.
127841.m: Screen readers read web pages aloud for blind people.

127842.q: What are the international WCAG guidelines for?
a: To make websites accessible to everyone
To make websites show more adverts
127842.e: WCAG stands for Web Content Accessibility Guidelines and comes from the W3C. The rules help to make websites accessible. Switzerland follows them too.
127842.m: The WCAG are the most important rules for accessible websites.

127843.q: Why is enough colour contrast between text and background important?
a: So that people with poor eyesight can read the text too
So that the page loads faster
So that the page uses less electricity
So that the domain becomes cheaper
127843.e: Light grey text on a white background is hard for many people to read. Strong contrast especially helps people with a visual impairment.
127843.m: Good contrast makes text readable for everyone.

127844.q: Why should a website also work without a mouse?
a: Because some people can only use the keyboard
Because web servers do not know about mice
127844.e: People with physical disabilities or blind people often use the computer with the keyboard only. With the Tab key they jump from element to element.
127844.m: A good website can be used with the keyboard alone.

127845.q: Why should you not show information only through colour, for example red boxes for errors?
a: Because some people cannot tell colours apart
Because red does not work on all screens
Because colours slow the page down
127845.e: People with colour blindness, for example, find it hard to tell red and green apart. That is why you add text or symbols to colours.
127845.m: Important messages need more than just a colour.

127846.q: What helps deaf people with videos on websites?
127846.e: Subtitles show what is said as text. That way deaf and hard of hearing people can understand the content.
127846.m: Subtitles make videos understandable for deaf people.

127847.q: Which Swiss law requires federal government websites to be accessible?
127847.e: The Disability Discrimination Act aims to prevent disadvantages for people with disabilities. It also obliges the federal government to make its online services accessible.
127847.m: In Switzerland, federal government websites must be accessible.

127848.q: Which HTML element starts a web form?
127848.e: All the input fields of a form are placed between <form> and </form>. The element also controls where the data is sent.
127848.m: A web form sits inside the form element.

127849.q: Which HTML element creates a single-line input field?
127849.e: <input type="text"> creates a single-line text field. With other types it becomes, for example, a date field or a button.
127849.m: Short entries are made with input.

127850.q: Which element is suitable for a longer text over several lines in a form?
127850.e: In a <textarea> you can write several lines, for example a message. Its size can be set with CSS or attributes.
127850.m: For long texts you use textarea.

127851.q: Which input type hides the characters you type behind dots?
127851.e: With type="password" the browser shows dots or asterisks instead of the characters. That way nobody looking at the screen can read along.
127851.m: Password fields have the type password.

127852.q: Which input type allows only exactly one choice out of several options?
127852.e: Radio buttons with the same name attribute form a group in which only one can be selected. With checkboxes you can tick several.
127852.m: With radio buttons you choose exactly one option.

127853.q: Which element links a label text to an input field?
127853.e: A <label> labels a field, and clicking on it activates the field. Screen readers connect the label to the field and read it out.
127853.m: Every input field should get a label.

127854.q: What does the required attribute do on an input field?
a: The field must be filled in
127854.e: With required, the browser only sends the form once the field is filled in. Otherwise a message appears.
127854.m: Required turns a field into a compulsory field.

127855.q: Which element creates a drop-down list?
127855.e: A <select> contains several <option> elements. You open the list and choose an entry, for example your canton.
127855.m: Drop-down lists are built with select and option.

127856.q: What can you do with JavaScript on a web page?
127856.e: With JavaScript a page reacts to clicks, checks entries or loads new content. HTML and CSS alone can hardly do that.

127857.q: Does JavaScript have anything to do with the programming language Java?
a: No, they are two different languages
Yes, it is the same language
Yes, JavaScript is an old version of Java
Yes, Java only runs with JavaScript
127857.e: Despite the similar name, Java and JavaScript are different languages. The name was chosen back then mainly for advertising reasons.
127857.m: Java and JavaScript are different languages despite their similar names.

127858.q: Which HTML element do you use to include JavaScript?
127858.e: JavaScript is placed in <script> elements or loaded from a file with <script src="file.js">. The browser then runs the code.
127858.m: JavaScript is included with the script element.

127859.q: What does console.log(2 + 3) show in the browser console?
127859.e: 2 and 3 are numbers, so JavaScript calculates 2 + 3 = 5. Only with text in quotation marks would the characters be joined together.
127859.m: JavaScript calculates with numbers quite normally.

127860.q: How do you write a one-line comment in JavaScript?
127860.e: The computer ignores everything after // up to the end of the line. Comments explain the code for humans.
127860.m: One-line comments in JavaScript start with two slashes.

127861.q: In modern JavaScript, which keyword creates a variable whose value is allowed to change?
127861.e: let number = 5; creates a variable that you can give a new value later. For values that should stay the same, you use const.
127861.m: Changeable variables are created with let.

127862.q: Where is JavaScript run on a normal web page?
127862.e: The browser has its own JavaScript engine that runs the code directly on the device. With Node.js, JavaScript can also run on servers.
127862.m: JavaScript usually runs directly in the browser.

127863.q: What does the comparison === mean in JavaScript?
a: Same value and same data type
127863.e: With ===, value and type must both match, so 5 === "5" is false. A single = on the other hand assigns a value.
127863.m: Three equals signs check value and type at the same time.

127864.q: In JavaScript, what do you call a function that runs when you click a button?
127864.e: An event handler reacts to events such as click or keydown. You connect it, for example, with addEventListener.
127864.m: JavaScript reacts to clicks with event handlers.

127865.q: You want to cross the road. What do you do first at the kerb?
127865.e: In Switzerland children learn: “Wait, look, listen, walk”. First you stop at the kerb, then you look and listen.

127866.q: What colour are zebra crossings in Switzerland?
127866.e: In Switzerland, zebra crossings are yellow. That makes them easy to see on the grey road.
127866.m: In Switzerland the zebra crossing is yellow.

127867.q: It is dark. What helps drivers see you better?
127867.e: Light colours and reflective strips shine in car headlights. That way the driver can see you from far away.
127867.m: Light and shiny means you are seen.

127868.q: Your ball rolls onto the road. What do you do?
127868.e: Children who run after a ball often forget about the cars. Stay at the side of the road and get help from a grown-up.
127868.m: No ball is as important as you.

127869.q: Mia's grandad falls over and does not wake up. Which number do you call?
127869.e: The number 144 calls the ambulance service. Paramedics help people who are ill or injured.

127870.q: What do you say on the phone when you call the emergency number?
a: Who you are, where you are and what has happened
127870.e: The helpers need to know where to come and what is going on. Stay calm and only hang up when they tell you to.
127870.m: Who, where, what: then help comes.

127871.q: Are you allowed to call the emergency number for fun?
a: No, only in a real emergency
Yes, if you hang up quickly
127871.e: If someone calls for fun, the line is busy. Then someone in real trouble might have to wait.
127871.m: An emergency call is not a game.

127872.q: What does the stop sign look like?
127872.e: The stop sign is red and has eight corners. Every vehicle must stop completely there.

127873.q: When is your bike helmet on properly?
a: It sits straight and the strap is fastened
It sits crooked at the back of your neck
127873.e: A helmet only protects you if it sits straight on your forehead and the chin strap is fastened. One finger should fit between the strap and your chin.
127873.m: Put it on straight, fasten the strap.

127874.q: Why does your bike have a bell?
127874.e: With the bell you show others that you are coming. That way pedestrians can make room for you.
127874.m: Ring ring means: watch out, here I come!

127875.q: Where does a banana skin go?
a: On the compost or in the green waste
127875.e: Banana skins are plant leftovers. On the compost they turn into new soil.

127876.q: Where do you take an empty jam jar?
127876.e: Glass can be melted down and made new. That is why it goes to the bottle bank.

127877.q: What do you do with a flat battery?
a: Take it to the collection box in a shop
127877.e: Batteries contain substances that harm nature. Every shop that sells batteries has a collection box.
127877.m: Flat batteries go back to the shop.

127878.q: You have an empty sweet wrapper in your hand. What do you do?
127878.e: Litter on the ground is bad for animals and looks ugly. If there is no bin, you take it home with you.

127879.q: What goes in the paper collection?
127879.e: Newspapers and exercise books are made of paper. New paper is made from waste paper.

127880.q: You meet your neighbour on the stairs. What do you say?
127880.e: In Switzerland people greet their neighbours in a friendly way with “Grüezi”. That makes living together nicer.

127881.q: It is late in the evening. Why do you play quietly now?
a: Because the neighbours want to sleep
Because otherwise the toys will break
Because you are never allowed to play in the evening
Because otherwise the lights go out
127881.e: In the evening and at night many people want to sleep. That is why everyone is quiet in the building then.
127881.m: At night the building is quiet.

127882.q: A stranger asks for your address in a chat. What do you do?
a: Give nothing away and show your parents
Send a photo of the house
127882.e: On the internet you can never be sure who is writing. Your address stays secret.

127883.q: Who is allowed to know your password?
127883.e: A password is like a key. Anyone who knows it can get into your account.

127884.q: You see a video online that frightens you. What do you do?
127884.e: If something frightens you, you can always talk about it. Grown-ups will help you.
127884.m: If something scares me, I tell someone.

127885.q: The bus stops. Who goes first?
127885.e: First people get off, then the others get on. That way there is no pushing.

127886.q: What do you need in the car to be safe?
a: A child seat and a seat belt
127886.e: In the car, children sit in a child seat and wear a seat belt. In an accident, this holds you in place.
127886.m: Belt up first, then drive off.

127887.q: A man you don't know wants to give you a lift in his car. What do you do?
127887.e: You never go with strangers, even if they are nice. Afterwards, tell your parents or your teacher.

127888.q: You find some matches. What do you do?
127888.e: A fire can start very quickly. That is why you give matches to a grown-up.

127889.q: Why is it dangerous to step into the road between parked cars?
a: Because the cars will drive off
Because it is too bright there
127889.e: Behind a car you are hidden from other drivers. It is better to cross where you can be seen clearly.
127889.m: If you are hidden, you are not seen.

127890.q: Where do pedestrians walk along a road?
a: In the middle of the road
127890.e: The pavement is the path for pedestrians next to the road. There you are protected from the cars.

127891.q: What does a triangular sign with a red border mean?
a: There is a cycle path here
127891.e: Triangular signs with a red border warn of danger. The picture in the middle shows what the danger is.
127891.m: A triangle with red means: be careful!

127892.q: A round blue sign shows a white bicycle. What does it mean?
a: There is a cycle path here
There is a bike shop here
127892.e: Round blue signs tell you what you must do. With a bike on it, the sign shows a cycle path.
127892.m: Blue and round with a bike: cycle path.

127893.q: A game on the tablet wants you to buy something. What do you do?
127893.e: Even in a game, a purchase like that costs real money. So always ask your parents first.
127893.m: Only buy things with your parents.

127894.q: You have lost your parents in the shopping centre. What do you do?
a: Ask a shop assistant at the till for help
127894.e: People who work in the shop are happy to help you. They can have your parents called over the loudspeaker.
127894.m: Lost? Ask someone who works there.

127895.q: You want to turn left on your bike. What do you do first?
a: Look behind you and stretch out your left arm
127895.e: With a hand signal you show others where you are going. Before that, look over your shoulder to check whether anyone is coming from behind.

127896.q: Which lights does a bike need at night?
a: White at the front, red at the back
Red at the front, white at the back
Blue at the front and back
Just one light on the helmet
